site.title: {page} · {site}
site.description: Party games for academics, played on everyone's phone: two research groups race to find their keywords, and whoever reveals Reviewer 2 is rejected.
site.hook: Reveal Reviewer 2, and your paper is rejected.
site.intro: Party games for academics, played on everyone's phone. In Double Blind, two research groups race to find their keywords: each group's PI gives a short clue and a number, and the students reveal cards. Reveal Reviewer 2, and your paper is rejected on the spot. 4–30 players, and joining a room needs no account. You can also play with Reviewer 1, an AI player.

found.1: Dear authors of the {group}, we are delighted to inform you that your submission has been accepted to R2Conf as an oral presentation. The reviewers were struck by how far ahead you finished: the other group still had {left} keywords to find. Please prepare a twelve-minute talk, and resist the urge to fit forty slides into it.
found.2: Dear {group}, congratulations! Out of a record number of submissions, yours is one of the very few selected for an oral at R2Conf. You found every keyword while your competitors still had {left} left on the table. The plenary hall is yours.
found.3: Dear {group}, the program committee is pleased to accept your paper as an oral presentation. Reviewer 2 looked hard for a weakness and found none. Your rivals are still looking for {left} keywords of their own.

reviewer2.1: Dear authors of the {group}, we are delighted to inform you that your submission has been accepted to R2Conf as an oral presentation. The competing paper from the {other} was assigned to Reviewer 2, and that was the end of it, with {left} keywords still to find. The stage is yours; please keep the talk under twelve minutes.
reviewer2.2: Dear {group}, congratulations! Your paper has been accepted for an oral at R2Conf. To be frank, the committee never got to compare the two papers: Reviewer 2 found the {other}'s first, {left} keywords from the finish line. A win is a win.
reviewer2.3: Dear {group}, the program committee is pleased to accept your paper as an oral presentation. The {other} turned over Reviewer 2 with {left} keywords still to find, and the slot went to you. Nobody will count how many you had found yourselves.

found.1: Dear {group}, we are pleased to inform you that your paper has been accepted to R2Conf as a spotlight. It was close: the other group had only {left} keywords left to find. You will have five minutes on stage; please use them wisely.
found.2: Dear {group}, congratulations on your acceptance with a spotlight presentation. The reviewers praised your clear clues and steady guessing, and noted that your rivals were just {left} keywords behind.
found.3: Dear {group}, your submission has been accepted as a spotlight paper. The area chair writes: “Solid work, finished with {left} keywords to spare on the other side. We expect the camera-ready version by Friday.”

reviewer2.1: Dear {group}, we are pleased to inform you that your paper has been accepted to R2Conf as a spotlight. The {other} was only {left} keywords from the finish when it ran into Reviewer 2. You will have five minutes on stage; please remember to thank the reviewer.
reviewer2.2: Dear {group}, congratulations on your acceptance with a spotlight presentation. It could have gone either way: the {other} had {left} keywords left when it found Reviewer 2 instead. The reviewers call this “a decisive contribution by the competition”.
reviewer2.3: Dear {group}, your submission has been accepted as a spotlight paper. The area chair writes: “The rival paper was {left} keywords short when Reviewer 2 got to it. Fortune favors the careful.” The camera-ready version is due on Friday.

found.1: Dear {group}, we are happy to let you know that your paper has been accepted to R2Conf as a poster. You won by a single keyword, which the reviewers called “a thrilling finish”. Please bring a poster tube and a strong voice.
found.2: Dear {group}, after a long discussion, your paper has been accepted as a poster. The other group was one keyword away from taking your slot. Posters are A0 and portrait; the coffee is at the back.
found.3: Dear {group}, congratulations: your paper squeezed in as a poster. One more keyword on the other side, and this letter would read very differently.

reviewer2.1: Dear {group}, we are happy to let you know that your paper has been accepted to R2Conf as a poster. The {other} was one keyword from the finish line, and turned over Reviewer 2 instead. Please bring a poster tube, and perhaps a thank-you card.
reviewer2.2: Dear {group}, after a short discussion, your paper has been accepted as a poster. The {other} needed one more keyword and found Reviewer 2 instead. The committee calls this “a narrow escape”. Posters are A0 and portrait.
reviewer2.3: Dear {group}, congratulations: your paper squeezed in as a poster. One more keyword for the {other}, and this letter would have gone to them. Reviewer 2 had other plans.

deskReject.1: Dear {group}, we regret to inform you that your submission has been desk rejected without review. Your group revealed Reviewer 2, who needed no further evidence. The {other} goes on to the conference without you.
deskReject.2: Dear {group}, your paper has been desk rejected. Reviewer 2 read the first line, wrote “major flaws throughout” and left. We wish you better luck in the next cycle.
deskReject.3: Dear {group}, thank you for your submission. Unfortunately, it was assigned to Reviewer 2, and that was the end of it: desk reject. The {other} sends its regards.

reject.1: Dear {group}, we regret to inform you that your paper was not accepted to R2Conf. The {other} found all of its keywords first, and there was room for only one of you. We received many strong submissions this year.
reject.2: Dear {group}, thank you for submitting to R2Conf. After careful consideration, the committee has decided to reject your paper. The {other} simply got there first. The reviews, all three words of them, are attached.
reject.3: Dear {group}, unfortunately your submission has been rejected. It was not a bad paper; the {other} just finished its paper sooner. We hope to see a revised version in the next game.

withdrawn.1: The chair withdrew this game before the end. The submission is closed: nobody is accepted, and nobody is rejected.
withdrawn.2: This submission has been withdrawn by the chair. No decision will be made, and no reviewer was harmed.
withdrawn.3: The chair pulled this paper before the decision. Both groups keep their keywords, and their dignity, for the next game.

letter.waitAgain: The chair can start another game.

explain.missed_deadline: For a PI whose time for a clue ran out before they gave one: the paper was written, it just never left the desktop. Earned again with every missed deadline, in each game that ends by itself while you are logged in and in your seat.
explain.deadline_hero: For a PI who gives a clue in the last 3 seconds of their time, when the students then find as many of the group's cards as it names before revealing anything else, or every card the group has left when fewer are left than the number; and for a student who reveals one of the group's cards in the last 3 seconds of the guesses: submitted at 23:59:57, and accepted. Earned again in every turn that makes you one, in each game with time limits that ends by itself while you are logged in and in your seat.
explain.opening_record: For everyone in a group whose very first clue of a game names 4 cards or more, and whose students then find that many of the group's cards before revealing anything else; a group that wins in that turn has the heavenly hand instead. The lab's first paper, accepted without a single revision.
explain.heavenly_hand: For everyone in a group that finds the last of its cards in the turn of its very first clue, and wins right there. One clue, one paper, straight into the journal of your dreams: the rarest title of all.
explain.instant_reject: For everyone in a group whose very first card was Reviewer 2, out on the spot. The paper came back before it had left the building.
explain.first_turn_reject: For everyone in a group whose students revealed Reviewer 2 in the turn of its very first clue, out on the spot; as the very first card, that is an instant desk reject instead. The lab's first paper, rejected before it ever reached review.

rules.roles: 4 to 12 players. The students share one term; Reviewer 2 gets a similar one and doesn't know it. A game of up to 8 has one Reviewer 2, and a game of 9 to 12 has {two}.
rules.pi: From 6 players there is a PI too, who gets no term, knows it, and has to bluff.
rules.win: Reviewer 2 wins by lasting until {small} players are left, or {large} in a game of 7 or more. If every Reviewer 2 is out while the PI is still in, the PI wins; once they are all out, the students win.
rules.comeback: Comeback: a Reviewer 2 or PI voted out has 30 seconds to guess the students' term once, and wins with a right guess.

describe.zh: In order of number, each player writes one line about their term, up to {count} characters.
describe.en: In order of number, each player writes one line about their term, up to {count} characters.

rules.giveaway: A line may not use any character of your term, a form of it, a translation or its pinyin, and may not all but repeat an earlier line.
rules.vote: After each round everyone votes at once, and the votes show together when all are in or time is up. You can't vote for yourself; abstaining scores 0, not voting in time −1. Whoever gets the most votes is out: their role shows, their term doesn't.
rules.tie: A tie: the tied players add a line each, and the others vote again among them; if it is still tied, nobody is out that round.
rules.anonymous: Seats show numbers alone; who had which shows at the end.
rules.time: Describing and voting have this room's time limits.
rules.noTime: This room has no time limits, for playing around one table.
rules.report: If someone breaks the rules, say by naming their term, tap their number to report them, with a reason. Everyone still in the game judges it within 20 seconds; with more than half agreeing, the player is out for breaking the rules, −3, and otherwise the reporter loses a point. One report a round each.
rules.offField: Those who are out, the spectators and the setter talk on the sidelines, which players still in the game can't see. No term of the game may be named there either.
rules.emotes: Players still in the game can't send reactions; once it is over, everyone can.
rules.points: Winning: students +3, Reviewer 2 +5, the PI +6; +1 for still being in at the end; +1 for each vote for a Reviewer 2 or the PI; +2 for a right comeback guess. Losing: −1 for each vote for a student who is voted out; −1 for a student voted out; −2 for a Reviewer 2 or PI out in the first round; −1 for a vote not cast in time; −3 for a line not written in time; −1 for a wrong comeback guess; −3 for breaking the rules; −1 for a rejected report.
rules.lost: A game with AI players, with someone removed, or ended early brings nobody points; it is recorded all the same.

game.scoring: Scores in a match: every own card that your group's students find, +1 for everyone in the group; winning, +3 for each student and +4 for the PI. Every irrelevant paper, card of the other group and Reviewer 2 that your students reveal, whoever of them it was, costs each student 1, 2 and 3, and the PI 2, 3 and 5. Every turn in which the PI gives no clue in time costs the PI 5. A big clue, with which the students find 4 of the group's cards or more: +1 for its PI for each from the fourth on. Opening the scoring, when the students find as many cards as the group's first clue names, 4 or more, before anything else: +1 for each student. A heavenly hand, winning in the turn of the first clue: +1 for each student, +3 for the PI, and no opening of the scoring besides.

rules.title: How to play
rules.defaults: These are the default settings. Each room can change them; the room's own settings apply.
rules.goal: Two research groups, red and blue, each have keywords hidden among the 25 cards on the board. The group that finds all of its keywords first wins.
rules.roles: Each group has one PI and as many students as it likes. The PIs see which cards belong to whom; the students see only the words.
rules.avatars: An avatar with a shadow can be tapped: it opens the player's page, or for a guest or an AI player, their panel.

turn.free: The PI gives a clue and a number: how many cards the clue points to, from 1 to the cards the group has left. The students then reveal cards one at a time, and go on for as long as they find their group's cards. Once they have revealed a card, they may end the turn.
turn.standard: The PI gives a clue and a number: how many cards the clue points to. The students then reveal cards one at a time, up to that number plus one. With 0 or ∞ there is no limit. Once they have revealed a card, they may end the turn.

rules.reveal: One of your group's cards: go on. An irrelevant paper or a card of the other group: your turn ends, and the other group's card counts for them. Reviewer 2: your paper is rejected, and your group loses at once.
rules.marks: A group's students may mark the cards still face down for each other, at any time: hold a card (or right-click it) to open its menu and pick ours, theirs or maybe Reviewer 2, and pick the same again to clear it (with the keyboard: 1, 2 and 3). A tap still chooses the card. The group's students and its PI see the marks; the PI can't set them.

clue.zh: A clue is one word of at most one character: a Chinese character counts as one, two letters or digits as one. An English word or abbreviation such as GPU is fine, but not the English for a word on the board, nor its pinyin. | A clue is one word of at most {count} characters: a Chinese character counts as one, two letters or digits as one. An English word or abbreviation such as GPU is fine, but not the English for a word on the board, nor its pinyin.
clue.en: A clue is one word. | A clue has at most {count} words.

rules.clueCommon: It can't be a word on the board, a part of one, or the card's term in the other language. The PI says nothing else and makes no gestures.
rules.clueCharacter: A number is the same character however it is written: 6, 六 and six. So are the English of a character and its pinyin, of three letters or more: ball and qiu are the same character as 球. With 大 on the board, big and great count as 大 too.

clueLetters.zh: A clue of letters alone gives away a Latin word on the board that has its letters in a row, capitals or not, at its start, in its middle or at its end, even a single letter: s and ts beside ETS, ai beside Email, s beside S波.
clueLetters.en: A clue of letters alone gives away a word on the board that starts with it, even a single letter: mode and m beside Model. Letters in the middle of a word don't count: art beside Earth is fine.

rules.clueSound: In a Chinese room, don't give a clue that sounds like a word on the board, such as 鸡音 (jīyīn) for 基因 (jīyīn, gene). The game doesn't check this: it's up to everyone to play fair.
rules.clueQuiet: While the students guess, neither group's PI may send a quick reaction, nor may anyone who has been a PI in this game.
rules.clueTargets: When giving a clue, the PI may tap cards to mark the ones it is meant for, and the number follows. Nobody sees the marks during the game; afterwards, the clue log and the replay show them.

clueRule.strict: This room's clue check is strict: a clue can't be another form of a word on the board that the word lists give, have a character in common with one, be letters that give one away, or, in a Chinese room, contain one. Other forms, which the check can only guess at, bring a warning, and the PI decides.
clueRule.loose: This room's clue check is loose: other forms of a word on the board, characters in common with one, letters that give one away, and clues that contain one only bring a warning, and the PI decides.

rules.time: The settings above say how much time each phase has. The bar under the turn shows what is left, and stays at the top of the screen when you scroll down.
rules.timeClue: A PI who gives no clue in time loses the turn to the other group, and 5 points of their own.
rules.timeGuess: Students whose time runs out end their turn, even if they have revealed nothing.
rules.extension: Each group may once a game ask for 30 seconds more for the phase it is in.
rules.pause: The chair can pause the game at any time. The board is hidden until the chair resumes it, and the clock goes on from where it stopped.
rules.noTime: This room has no time limits.
rules.end: A group wins as soon as all its cards are revealed, even when the other group revealed the last one.

coauthor.2: A good collaborator is harder to find than a good topic.

privacy.guestNotice: Games are recorded, the chats included, to train AI players and for research; nothing published carries names.
privacy.records: Games are recorded, with what the players say in their chats, the reports they make in them, how they rate a game or guess its AI players, and the words they give for one, which may be adopted into the word library. The records are used to train and test the game's AI players, and may be used for research and published as a dataset, without names or accounts. The players with accounts can watch a finished game again, without the chats. A replay keeps no name: it shows each account as it is now, with its username and avatar, a deleted account as a deleted player, and guests by their numbers in the room. If you delete your account, the replays show you as a deleted player, and what you said in the games stays, anonymous like the rest of the records and no longer linked to you.

rules.title: The rules in brief
rules.about: The goal, roles, a turn, revealing, clues, time, the end

1.title: The goal
1.body: In short: the first group to reveal all its keywords wins.

2.title: Roles
2.body: PIs see the colors and only give clues; students don't, and do the revealing.

3.title: A turn
3.body: The PI gives a word and a number; the students reveal cards one at a time.

4.title: Revealing
4.body: Right: go on. Wrong: the turn passes. Reviewer 2: you lose.

5.title: Clues
5.body: Not a word on the board, a part of one, or the same word in the other language.

6.title: Time
6.body: Clues and guesses have time limits; when time runs out, the turn is over.

7.title: The end
7.body: Once all your cards are revealed you win, even if the others revealed the last one. Rooms can change these rules: see "Room settings".

student.title: Playing a student
student.about: Read the PI's clue and reveal cards with your group

1.title: You're a student
1.body: You're a student in the red group, and only the PI sees the colors. Red has 9 cards, blue 8: the first group to reveal all its own wins. The strip at the top is red: it's your group's turn. Wait for your PI's clue.

2.title: The clue
2.body: The clue is "Astronomy, 3": three of red's cards have to do with astronomy. You may go on as long as you're right; the number is only a hint.

3.title: Choose a card
3.body: Which card fits best? Tap "Black hole" to choose it. Your group sees your choice; if you're unsure, talk it over in the group chat.

4.title: Reveal it
4.body: Once you're sure, tap "Reveal". There's no taking it back.

5.title: Right!
5.body: Black hole is red! Right guesses let you go on: tap "Telescope".

6.title: One more
6.body: Telescope is right too. For the third you chose "Dark matter": tap "Reveal".

7.title: An irrelevant paper
7.body: Dark matter is an irrelevant paper: it counts for nobody, but your turn is over and blue plays, so the strip at the top turns white again.

8.title: The other group's turn
8.body: Blue is guessing "Statistics, 2". Meanwhile, hold a card down to mark it for your group, such as "P-value" as theirs.

9.title: They got one wrong
9.body: Blue revealed "Galaxy", a red card: it counts for you, and blue's turn is over.

10.title: Quit while ahead
10.body: The clue is "Biology, 3" and you have two right. Unsure of a third? Tap "End the turn" rather than risk it.

11.title: Reviewer 2
11.body: Blue revealed "Deadline", which was Reviewer 2: the group that reveals it is rejected on the spot, so red is accepted! You can't see colors, so think before every reveal.

12.title: Looking back
12.body: Two ways to win: reveal all your cards first, or have the others reveal Reviewer 2. After every game, the clue log shows the cards the PI meant with each clue.

pi.title: Playing the PI
pi.about: See the colors, give one word and a number

1.title: You see the colors
1.body: You're the red group's PI. Cards tagged "Red" are your group's, "Blue" the other group's, "Irrelevant" are irrelevant papers, and "R2" is Reviewer 2. Students see only the words.

2.title: Mark the cards you mean
2.body: Tap cards to circle the ones your clue means, and the number follows. The circles stay hidden until the game ends. Black hole and Telescope are circled: tap "Galaxy" too.

3.title: No words from the board
3.body: A clue can't be a word on the board or a part of one. "Galaxy" is refused: try another.

4.title: Give the clue
4.body: Make it "Astronomy": it fits all three. Tap "Give the clue".

5.title: Watch them guess
5.body: Once the clue is out, you only watch: no talking, no gestures. You see which card your students choose, and you can read the group chat but not write in it.

6.title: Prepare the next one
6.body: During the other group's turn you can draft your next clue. Only you see it, and you give it once it's your turn.

7.title: The clock
7.body: You have 2 minutes for the first clue and 90 seconds for each later one; the clock turns red when it's your move. Run out and the turn passes to the other group, and you lose 5 points.

8.title: The end
8.body: When the game ends, the clue log shows the cards you circled with each clue and how many your students found.

extras.title: More in a game
extras.about: Group chat, marks, reactions, extensions, pausing, replays

1.title: Group chat
1.body: Students talk it over in the group chat, which only their group sees. The PI can read it but not write: the clue is all a PI may say.

2.title: Marks
2.body: Hold a card down (or right-click it) for its menu: ours, theirs or R2?. Pick the same again to clear it; on a computer, keys 1, 2 and 3 work too.

3.title: Reactions
3.body: Tap "React" to send a quick reaction that everyone in the room and every big screen sees and hears, once every 10 seconds. PIs can't react while students guess. Too noisy? Mute the sounds in the room menu.

4.title: Time and extensions
4.body: The clock at the top shows the time left in this phase. If the room allows extensions, each group may once a game ask for 30 seconds more.

5.title: Pausing and dropping out
5.body: The chair can pause at any time. If you drop out, refresh or open the link again to get your seat back; in a room with Reviewer 1, an AI plays for you if you're gone for 20 seconds in your turn.

6.title: Review and replay
6.body: After a game, "Review the game" opens its replay, and your group can keep talking it over until the next game. With an account you can watch it again later from your record.

settings.title: Room settings
settings.about: Guessing, clue checks, time limits, word lists

1.title: Guessing
1.body: "Free": students go on as long as they're right, and the PI's number is only a hint. "Standard": at most the number plus one. Free is the default.

2.title: Clue check
2.body: "Strict" refuses a clue too close to a word on the board, such as one sharing a character with it; "Loose" only warns. Strict is the default.

3.title: Clue length
3.body: A Chinese room allows 4 characters by default, two letters or digits counting as one; an English room allows one word.

4.title: Time limits and extensions
4.body: By default: 120 seconds for the first clue, 90 for each later one and 120 for guessing; 0 means no limit. Extensions are off by default.

5.title: Word lists and your own words
5.body: Choose the word lists when you make a room, or let each game draw them anew. In a private room, the chair can add their own words at the chair's desk in the waiting room.

account.title: Your account and page
account.about: Signing up, your avatar, what your page shows

1.title: Registering
1.body: Registering takes only a username and a password, no email. An account lets you make public rooms, play with Reviewer 1, add friends and earn ranks.

2.title: Avatar and name
2.body: On your account page, upload a picture and drag it into the circle for your avatar; you can rename yourself there too.

3.title: Your public page
3.body: Anyone can open your public page and see your username, avatar, rank and titles. Whether it shows your record and feedback contributions, and what link and one-line bio it has, is up to you.

4.title: Email and password
4.body: Add an email address, so that a forgotten password can be reset.

rooms.title: Rooms and invitations
rooms.about: The choices for a new room, and inviting friends

1.title: Language and word lists
1.body: Tap "New room", then choose the language, which the cards follow too, and at least one word list.

2.title: Ordinary room or match
2.body: An ordinary room plays as many games as you like; a match plays a set number, scores everyone and ranks them at the end.

3.title: Public or private
3.body: Private: only those with the number or the link get in. Public: listed on the home page, for anyone with an account to join.

4.title: Play or watch
4.body: "Play" gives you a seat as you come in; "Watch" just watches. You can change later.

5.title: Share the room
5.body: A room's number looks like R2-K7QX. Share it, copy the link or show the QR code; friends can also type the number on the home page. "Big screen" puts the game on a big screen.

6.title: Invite friends
6.body: With an account, "Invite friends" calls your friends straight in, for 10 minutes; friends can also ask to join your room from "Friends playing" on the home page.

lobby.title: The waiting room
lobby.about: Seats, starting, the chair's desk, Reviewer 1 in empty seats

1.title: Taking a seat
1.body: Each group has one PI and any number of students. Tap "Be the PI" or "Join as a student", or "Watch".

2.title: Starting
2.body: Once both groups have an online PI and at least one student, the chair can tap "Start", or "Shuffle groups" first.

3.title: The chair's desk
3.body: At the chair's desk the chair changes the word lists and the rules, and in a private room adds their own words. The chair can also hand the role to someone else.

4.title: Not enough people?
4.body: On the home page, "Play with Reviewer 1" with "With friends" opens a room where Reviewer 1 can take the seats nobody takes.

more.title: Friends, ranks, titles, streaks
more.about: What they are and where to find them

1.title: Friends
1.body: On your account page, find people by username or page link and send a request; you can give friends a note only you see. In a room, tap a player to add them too.

2.title: Academic ranks
2.body: Every game you finish in a seat while logged in earns points, from "Kindergartner" all the way to "Reviewer 2". Games with an AI earn none.

3.title: Titles and streaks
3.body: Special games earn titles, such as "Heavenly Hand" or "Deadline Hero", and three wins in a row make "3 Submissions, 3 Acceptances". Tap a title to see how it's earned.

4.title: Friend titles
4.body: After 3 games with the same friend you may earn a friend title, such as "Co-First Author", that only you see.

feedback.title: Giving feedback
feedback.about: Where to tell us an idea or a problem

1.title: Sending feedback
1.body: There's "Feedback" at the bottom of the home page and "Send feedback" in a room's menu: choose what it's about (an idea, a new game, a bug or the word lists), write it, and leave a contact if you like.

2.title: Once adopted
2.body: Adopted feedback is listed under "Feedback contributions" on the home page, by name or anonymously, as you chose.
